summary: This RFC describes the DCN protocols for keeping connectivity, routing, and clock information in a local network. It was published as an example that designers and implementers of other local networks might find useful.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 891 describes how DCN hosts exchange information to maintain local connectivity, choose routes, and keep clocks synchronized. Each host measures its links and updates its own tables, within a design intended for small local networks.

questions: what are the dcn local network protocols
how does dcn handle routing and clock information
what is the dcn hello protocol
how does dcn calculate roundtrip delay
subtitle: How DCN hosts exchange neighbor, routing, delay, and clock information.

tldr.problem: A small local network needs to maintain reachability, choose routes, and synchronize clocks without a central routing controller.
tldr.mechanism: Neighboring hosts exchange HELLO messages with delay, clock-offset, and host-table information. Each host measures round-trip delay and updates routes toward the minimum-delay paths.
tldr.outcome: The design is for local networks of up to 256 hosts and gateways. The RFC presents it as an example for designers of other networks.

today: RFC 891 is listed as an Internet Standard and was published in December 1983. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The DCN Local Network
sections.content:
The Distributed Computer Network (DCN) uses Internet technology and Fuzzball software on connected hosts. Each host can provide packet switching, gateway, and service functions, while hosts organize routes around measured delay.

The design targets local networks of up to 256 hosts and gateways. The RFC says it is not intended for large, complex networks or the advanced routing and control algorithms of the ARPANET.
sections.plainLanguage: DCN is a local network where hosts organize connectivity and routing among themselves. The described design is intended for a limited-size network, not a large backbone.

sections.title: Host and Network Tables
sections.content:
Each host maintains a Host Table indexed by host ID and a Net Table for other networks. The Host Table records delay, clock offset, outgoing port, update time, and a TTL for each virtual host.

The Net Table maps a network number to a gateway host ID. Most entries are configured; a host running a GGP/EGP gateway process can maintain its entries through gateway operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each host keeps one table for routes to local virtual hosts and another for gateways to other networks. HELLO messages update the local host information.

sections.title: HELLO Messages
sections.content:
A HELLO is an IP datagram using protocol number 63. Its fixed area contains a checksum, date, time, timestamp, address offset, and host count; a host area can carry delay and clock-offset information for each host.

A message sent to a host on the same local network includes both areas. Other HELLO messages carry only the fixed area. The message timestamp supports round-trip delay measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: A HELLO message reports the sender's time and routing measurements. When neighbors share a local network, it can also include the sender's host table information.

sections.title: Measuring Delay and Choosing Routes
sections.content:
Hosts exchange HELLO messages on shared links. Echoed timestamps let a host compute round-trip delay without relying on the two hosts' clock offsets. The host adds the measured delay to the values reported by a neighbor and compares the results with its Host Table.

A different link replaces the current route only when it is better by at least the switching threshold, currently 100 milliseconds. A calculated delay above 30 seconds marks a host down, while values below 100 milliseconds are treated as 100 milliseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Each host estimates how long a route takes and prefers a lower-delay route. It switches to a different link only when the measured improvement reaches the configured threshold.

sections.title: Timeouts and HELLO Timing
sections.content:
A Host Table entry has a TTL that is decremented once per second. The current value is 120 seconds; if no update arrives before it expires, the host is declared down. HELLO intervals range from about eight to 30 seconds, depending on link speed.

IP datagram TTL is set to 30, which limits the maximum path delay to 30 seconds. A minimum delay of 100 milliseconds reduces unnecessary route changes caused by small measurement variations.
sections.plainLanguage: A host is declared down when its table entry expires without a fresh update. HELLO timing and the minimum route-change threshold help the network distinguish silence and meaningful path improvements.

sections.title: Clock Synchronization
sections.content:
The design maintains physical, apparent, and actual clocks. The logical clocks run at 1000 Hz and reset at midnight UT. A host uses the selected master clock host's valid time information to correct its own clock.

Small corrections are slewed gradually to keep apparent time increasing. A large correction is applied as a step and starts a hold interval during which timestamps are treated as invalid and delay calculations are suppressed.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts use time information from a designated master and adjust their local clocks. Small corrections are gradual; after a large correction, the system waits before trusting timestamps again.
